passages.t: The king rejoices, and ‘Be exalted, O LORD’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). Psalm 20 prayed for the king before battle. Psalm 21 gives thanks after it. “O LORD, the king rejoices in Your strength. How greatly he exults in Your salvation!” (verse 1).

God has answered. “You have granted his heart's desire” (verse 2). God “placed on his head a crown of pure gold” (verse 3). “He asked You for life, and You granted it” (verse 4).

The reason is in the middle: “For the king trusts in the LORD; through the loving devotion of the Most High, he will not be shaken” (verse 7).

Then the psalm turns to the king's enemies, in fierce words: God will “place them in a fiery furnace at the time of Your appearing” (verse 9). It ends in praise of God, not the king: “Be exalted, O LORD, in Your strength; we will sing and praise Your power” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
This is a royal psalm, the twin of Psalm 20. The first verse and the last both speak of God's ‘strength’, so the king's joy is framed by God's power.

‘Length of days, forever and ever’ (verse 4) was the language of royal courts. Bathsheba said to David, “May my lord King David live forever!” (1 Kings 1:31). It was a prayer for a long reign and a lasting family line. In Israel it carried more weight, because God had promised David a throne “established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16).

The ‘fiery furnace’ of verse 9 is in Hebrew a household oven, the clay bread oven heated until it glowed. It is a picture of judgment that is swift and complete.
passages.later:
No king of David's line lived forever. Their line ended in exile in Babylon. The early church read the language of verses 3 to 6 as fulfilled in Jesus, whom God raised to reign forever. Hebrews speaks of Jesus “now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death” (Hebrews 2:9). Revelation pictures him with “many royal crowns on His head” (Revelation 19:12).

The God who grants the king ‘life’ (verse 4) is the God of whom Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).
passages.hard: Verses 8 to 12 speak of God destroying the king's enemies, even their descendants (verse 10). These are words about the enemies of God's king, spoken to God, and they belong with the hard lines the book page treats in ‘The cursing psalms’. No reading of them makes it right to harm anyone, and no modern nation or army stands in the place of Israel's anointed king.
passages.asks:
Psalm 20 asked; Psalm 21 thanks. The pair asks whether you come back to thank God after the trouble passes, or only pray before it.

Notice also where the psalm ends. The king is glad, but the last line praises God, not the king. Every success you have can end the same way.
